description: Learning by diving into a wealth of information always accelerates growth!
summary:
Orbitect is a browser game that puts players in charge of a real space mission, from the first need to the final verdict. Players pick a need NASA faces, such as spotting new wildfires or following tropical cyclones, and set their own full and minimum success targets. They then build the spacecraft in eight steps: sensor, body, power, pointing, computer, communications, thruster and rocket. Every choice pulls on six live margins: mass, power, budget, data, signal and time. These are sized to NASA Goddard's engineering standard (GSFC-STD-1000).

At launch, a short film flies the design against frozen NASA records. Every event the game scores against comes from NASA: 600 FIRMS fire detections and three cyclones tracked by EONET in November 2026, plus space weather events from DONKI in 2024. The debrief names the cause in numbers and suggests the one change to try. It also replays the same design 60 times, so players can tell bad luck from bad design. One to four players can share one screen, each owning part of the spacecraft.

Orbitect turns abstract trade-offs into decisions players feel, and teaches why missions succeed or fail, not just whether they do.
details:
What it does

Orbitect lets anyone design a space mission and see it fly. The player picks a real need, such as wildfires or tropical cyclones, and sets targets for full and minimum success. They build the spacecraft in eight steps (sensor, body, power, pointing, computer, communications, thruster, rocket) on a live 3D model. Six linked resources react to every choice: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. At launch, one physics model flies the design against real NASA records (FIRMS fires, EONET cyclones, DONKI space weather), plays a short film of the flight, and ends with a debrief that names the cause, the numbers and the one change to try.

Benefits

- Players learn by doing: every trade-off has a visible cost.

- Players learn why: each result traces back to their own choices.

- Players can trust it: the physics was checked against 15 figures from 5 missions NASA has flown (median error 0.07%).

- It runs in any browser as one file, even offline.

Intended impact

To show students, especially those choosing a major, how space agencies think, and to build three skills: setting a goal in numbers, balancing a whole system, and explaining a result.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework. Three.js for the 3D spacecraft, Canvas 2D for the flight film and maps. NASA data was downloaded once and frozen inside the game. Playwright was used for automated play tests. No special hardware: it runs on a laptop or phone. Code and text were written with AI assistance (Claude).

Creativity

- Missions are tested on real events, not invented scores.

- A short film shows the moment that decided the mission.

- Each design is flown 60 times, so players can tell bad luck from bad design.

- One to four players share one screen, each owning part of the spacecraft.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: every number is labelled as read in a NASA source, a standard value, or a game value.

- Plain language: full names first, with short descriptions for beginners.

- Access: works on phones and offline, with reduced motion supported.

- Honesty: costs and failure odds are game values, and we say so.
